title: PARTITION BY and window frames
objective: Control exactly which rows a window function sees: PARTITION BY for groups, ORDER BY for sequence, and ROWS/RANGE frames for running totals, moving averages and first/last values.
context: Finance wants share-of-total and year-to-date revenue; merchandising wants each product's share of its category; the growth team wants 3-month moving averages that smooth noisy months. These are all 'aggregate over a sliding set of rows while keeping every row' — window frames.

exercises.title: Category share of total revenue
exercises.question: The CEO asks: what share of our revenue does each category bring in?
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return category (use 'Uncategorized' when products.category is NULL), revenue (rounded to 2) and pct_of_total (the category's revenue as a percentage of all revenue, 0–100 scale, rounded to 1 decimal).
hints: An empty OVER () means 'all rows of the result'.
After GROUP BY, SUM(SUM(x)) OVER () is the grand total of the group sums.
ROUND(100.0 * SUM(qty*price) / SUM(SUM(qty*price)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total ... GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category,'Uncategorized')
exercises.why: Share-of-total without a second query or a cross join to a totals CTE. The percentages always add up (to rounding) to 100.

recall.q: What does SUM(SUM(x)) OVER () compute in a GROUP BY query?
recall.a: The window SUM over all grouped rows of the per-group SUMs — i.e. the grand total, repeated on each row.

exercises.title: Product share within its category
exercises.question: Category managers want to know which products carry their category.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). For every product with revenue, return product_id, product_name, category ('Uncategorized' when NULL), product_revenue (rounded 2), category_revenue (total revenue of that category, rounded 2) and pct_of_category (product_revenue as a 0–100 percentage of category_revenue, rounded to 1 decimal).
hints: One row per product first (CTE), then a window partitioned by category.
SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category) puts the category total on each product row.
ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category), 1) AS pct_of_category
exercises.why: PARTITION BY without ORDER BY gives a group total on every row — no join back to a category-totals table needed.

recall.q: What frame does SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g) use when there is no ORDER BY?
recall.a: The whole partition — every row of the group.

exercises.snowflake: RATIO_TO_REPORT(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category) returns the 0–1 share directly.

exercises.title: Customer cumulative spend
exercises.question: Loyalty wants each order annotated with the customer's spend to date and how far along their lifetime spend that order put them.
exercises.prompt: Order value = SUM(quantity * unit_price) of the order's lines, valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_value (rounded 2), cumulative_spend (the customer's running total of order_value up to and including this order, ordering by order_date then order_id; rounded 2) and pct_of_lifetime (cumulative_spend as a 0–100 percentage of the customer's total spend over all their valid orders, rounded to 1 decimal).
hints: Two windows on the same partition: one with ORDER BY + frame (running), one without (total).
SUM(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Put both windows in a CTE, then ROUND(100.0 * cumulative_spend / lifetime_spend, 1) outside.
exercises.why: Running totals per entity drive loyalty tiers ('crossed $500 lifetime') and LTV curves.

recall.q: What's the difference between SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY c) and SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY c ORDER BY d)?
recall.a: Without ORDER BY you get the partition total on every row; with ORDER BY the default frame makes it a running total.

exercises.title: Year-to-date revenue by month
exercises.question: Finance tracks revenue YTD: the running total must reset every January.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return month ('YYYY-MM'), revenue (rounded 2) and ytd_revenue (running total of revenue within the same calendar year up to and including this month, rounded 2), for all months 2024-01…2025-12. Order by month.
hints: The running total must restart each year: that's a PARTITION BY.
The year is substr(month, 1, 4) — you can partition by an expression.
SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY substr(month,1,4) ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
exercises.why: PARTITION BY resets the running total; that one clause turns 'cumulative since launch' into 'YTD'.

recall.q: Which clause makes a running total restart each year?
recall.a: PARTITION BY year — the window never crosses partition boundaries.

exercises.snowflake: SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY YEAR(month) ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), with month = DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date).

exercises.title: 3-month moving average
exercises.question: Monthly revenue is noisy (March 2025 was tiny). The growth team wants a trailing 3-month average.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return month ('YYYY-MM'), revenue (rounded 2), moving_avg_3m (average revenue of this month and the two previous months, rounded 2 — for the first two months average whatever months exist) and months_in_window (how many months that average used: 1, 2 or 3). Order by month.
hints: A sliding frame: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
COUNT(*) over the same frame tells you how many rows were really averaged.
AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg_3m, COUNT(*) OVER (same) AS months_in_window
exercises.why: Moving averages are how trends get shown to executives. months_in_window tells readers which early values are based on less data (many dashboards blank those out).

recall.q: What does ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW include?
recall.a: The current row plus up to two rows before it in the window order — at most 3 rows.

exercises.title: ROWS vs RANGE on tied dates
exercises.question: An analyst's running total 'jumps' several lines at once. Show Q4 2025 order lines with both frame types side by side.
exercises.prompt: Take order lines of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) with order_date between '2025-10-01' and '2025-12-31'. Return order_item_id, order_id, order_date, line_revenue (quantity * unit_price, rounded 2), running_rows (running SUM of line revenue ordered by order_date, order_item_id with a ROWS frame from the first row to the current row, rounded 2) and running_range (running SUM of line revenue ordered by order_date ONLY, using RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, rounded 2). Order by order_date, order_item_id.
hints: Same SUM, two different OVER clauses.
RANGE treats all rows with the same order_date as peers: they all get the total through the end of that date.
SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY o.order_date, oi.order_item_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) vs SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY o.order_date RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
exercises.why: The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE. If your ORDER BY has ties, a 'running total' silently includes future peer rows — compare the two columns on multi-line orders.

recall.q: Two rows tie on the ORDER BY value. Under RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, does the first one include the second in its frame?
recall.a: Yes — RANGE includes all peers of the current row; ROWS stops at the physical current row.

exercises.title: First and latest order value (LAST_VALUE pitfall)
exercises.question: For every order, sales wants the customer's first-ever order value and their most recent order value side by side.
exercises.prompt: Order value = SUM(quantity * unit_price) of the order's lines, valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_value (rounded 2), first_order_value (order_value of the customer's earliest valid order) and latest_order_value (order_value of the customer's most recent valid order — the same value on all of that customer's rows). Order a customer's orders by order_date then order_id.
hints: FIRST_VALUE works with the default frame (it always starts at the first row). LAST_VALUE does not.
Default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so LAST_VALUE would return the current order. Extend it to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
LAST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
exercises.why: This is the single most common window-function bug in production dashboards. An alternative that dodges it: FIRST_VALUE(...) OVER (... ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC).

recall.q: Why does LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (PARTITION BY c ORDER BY d) usually return the current row's x?
recall.a: Because with ORDER BY the default frame ends at the current row, so the 'last' row of the frame is the current one.

exercises.snowflake: Same frame fix in Snowflake; or use FIRST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC).

worked_example.question: Show 2025 monthly revenue with a running total for the year.
worked_example.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
      AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_revenue
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
worked_example.explanation: The frame starts at the first month and ends at the current one, so each row adds its month to everything before it. Here the 2025 filter is fine *before* the window because we want the running total to start in January 2025.

recipe:
**Recipe: a window = partition + order + frame**

1. `SUM(x) OVER ()` — the whole result set. Great for **share of total**: `x / SUM(x) OVER ()`.
2. `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)` — total of the row's group, repeated on every row (share within group).
3. Add `ORDER BY` and the default frame becomes `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
   → a **running total**. RANGE includes all *peers* (rows with the same ORDER BY value).
4. Say exactly what you mean with an explicit frame:

```sql
SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY yr ORDER BY month
                   ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)   -- running / YTD
AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                   ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)           -- 3-period moving avg
LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY t
                   ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) -- true last value
```

**ROWS vs RANGE:** ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups rows with equal ORDER BY values. With ties
(several lines on the same date) a RANGE running total jumps by the whole day at once.

**FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE pitfall:** with ORDER BY and the default frame, the frame ends at the current
row — so LAST_VALUE just returns the current row. Always widen the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

**Windows over aggregates:** `SUM(SUM(x)) OVER ()` is legal — the inner SUM is the GROUP BY aggregate,
the outer one is the window over the grouped rows.
snowflake_notes:
Window frames are identical in Snowflake (`ROWS`/`RANGE BETWEEN ... PRECEDING/FOLLOWING`), plus:

- `RATIO_TO_REPORT(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` = share of total as a 0–1 fraction, in one call.
- `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` / `YEAR(order_date)` for buckets and partitions:

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS month,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)  AS revenue,
       SUM(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)) OVER (
           PARTITION BY YEAR(month) ORDER BY month
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ytd_revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY 1;
```

- `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '30 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (value-based frames on dates) is supported in
  Snowflake; SQLite supports numeric RANGE offsets only (e.g. on `julianday(order_date)`).
- `FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE/NTH_VALUE` have the same default-frame pitfall in Snowflake. `IGNORE NULLS` is available.
common_mistakes: Relying on the default frame: with ORDER BY it is RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, which includes tied peers.
LAST_VALUE without ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — returns the current row.
Computing share of total with a window over line-level rows but grouping later — aggregate first or use SUM(SUM(x)) OVER ().
Forgetting PARTITION BY year for YTD, so the running total never resets.
Assuming ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING means '3 months' when months can be missing — it means 3 rows.
recall: What is the default window frame when ORDER BY is present? And when it is absent?
With ORDER BY: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Without: the whole partition.
Write the frame for a 3-row trailing moving average.
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
How do you compute each row's share of its group total in one pass?
x / SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY group) — or RATIO_TO_REPORT(x) OVER (PARTITION BY group) in Snowflake.
ROWS vs RANGE in one sentence?
ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE treats rows with equal ORDER BY values as one block (peers).
